### Observed differences

- The elapsed time between consecutive completion events for the activity pair A22 → A23 roughly halved. In the earlier window a typical gap was about 1.0 hours (median about 1.02 h; the middle half of cases between about 0.87 and 1.12 h); in the later window a typical gap was about 0.5 hours (median about 0.50 h; middle half between about 0.45 and 0.56 h) — about half an hour less in the typical case. [TWAIT001]
- The whole gap distribution shifted down and tightened together: mean, median and both quartiles all decreased, and the spread narrowed from a standard deviation of about 0.16 h to about 0.09 h. The gap was observed in all 200 traces of each window, and the difference is larger than in about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [TWAIT001]
- This timing gap was the only item that qualified across the 69 tested units: no control-flow, ordering or participation difference passed screening (0 items, against about 0.27 expected by chance if nothing had changed). [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence

The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process. The single A22 → A23 timing item is the only qualifying finding, and with about 0.007 time items expected by chance in that family, one isolated item — however large or unusual it looks — is what an unchanged process typically produces at these thresholds, a reading consistent with the empty control-flow family (0 items against about 0.27 expected). [TWAIT001]

Here we have 1 item in the time family when 0.007 is expected. That's one item when fewer than one is expected. According to the rule, that's "a count of the same order as that expectation"? So per the rule, we should choose "Insufficient evidence", however large or unusual a single item looks.

A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole, even when all items describe one underlying difference; do not merge items for this comparison."

Hmm, there's tension. 1 item vs 0.007 expected — 1 is many times larger than 0.007 (143x). But the example says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is the same order. The example is unambiguous: one item when fewer than one is expected → Insufficient evidence. The instruction is designed to be conservative. So the answer is Insufficient evidence.

The example bounds "same order" at one or two items when expectation < 1. So 1 item with 0.007 expected → same order per the example → Insufficient evidence.
